questions.question: In group terms, what is the kernel of a homomorphism φ: E → E' ?
options: The set of points that map to the identity element (the point at infinity)
The set of points where the curve equation has no solutions
The set of points with x = 0
The set of points with maximal order
questions.explanation: The kernel is exactly the set of inputs that map to the group identity; for elliptic curves that identity is the point at infinity.

questions.question: On a short Weierstrass curve y^2 = x^3 + ax + b over a prime field, what characterizes a 2-torsion point (order 2) in affine coordinates?
options: It has y = 0 (so the point is its own negation)
It has x = 0
It has y = 1
It has x = y
questions.explanation: In short Weierstrass form, negation is (x, y) → (x, -y), so a point equals its negation exactly when y = 0.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes an isogeny from an isomorphism?
options: An isogeny can be many-to-one (non-injective) because it collapses a finite kernel; an isomorphism is bijective
An isogeny is only defined over the real numbers; an isomorphism is only defined over finite fields
An isogeny preserves x-coordinates; an isomorphism preserves y-coordinates
An isogeny always has degree 1; an isomorphism always has prime degree
questions.explanation: Isogenies are homomorphisms with finite kernel and typically are not invertible; isomorphisms are reversible coordinate changes.

questions.question: In the short-Weierstrass Vélu setup used in this lesson, which codomain update is correct?
questions.explanation: Vélu’s formulas compute v and w from the kernel representatives and update the curve coefficients with the (a - 5v, b - 7w) rule.

questions.question: What should φ(Q) be for any kernel point Q ∈ ker(φ) ?
options: The point at infinity (the identity), because kernel points are exactly those mapped to identity
Q itself (kernel points are fixed points)
A random point on the codomain curve
A point with y = 0 on the codomain curve
questions.explanation: By definition, the kernel is the set of points that map to the identity element.

questions.question: Why does Vélu’s construction use a set S containing one representative from each ± pair of non-2-torsion kernel points (plus all 2-torsion points)?
options: To avoid double-counting Q and -Q while keeping the sums well-defined and covering the whole kernel structure
Because only one point in each ± pair lies on the curve
Because it makes the isogeny injective
Because it ensures the curve becomes singular
questions.explanation: Non-2-torsion kernel points come in ± pairs; summing over one representative per pair avoids duplicating contributions.

questions.question: You find SIDH/SIKE used for key establishment in a production system. What is the correct posture today?
options: Treat it as broken for security purposes, plan removal, rotate affected secrets, and migrate to supported PQ KEMs
Keep it; isogeny-based cryptography is automatically post-quantum safe forever
Only increase parameter sizes; the underlying protocol design is unaffected
Replace it with a custom curve and keep the same SIDH protocol
questions.explanation: SIDH/SIKE suffered efficient key-recovery attacks; migration should prioritize removing broken primitives and rotating impacted material.

questions.question: If your goal is post-quantum key establishment in real systems, what is the most practical replacement direction?
options: Adopt standardized PQ KEMs (e.g., ML-KEM), often in a hybrid transition if needed
Implement SIDH from scratch in Python and deploy it behind TLS
Use elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman with a larger curve
Use RSA-4096 as a post-quantum KEM
questions.explanation: For engineering migration, the path is standardized PQ KEMs with crypto-agility; toy implementations and broken designs are not acceptable.
